source.title: Scaling deep learning for materials discovery
source.authors: Amil Merchant; Simon Batzner; S. Schoenholz; M. Aykol; Gowoon Cheon; E. Cubuk

record.file_problem: None; the full article and methods are present. Some equation formatting shows PDF extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Tests data-scaling behavior in materials-science models, extending scaling-law results to a different scientific domain and different error measures.
record.gate_note: The study does not test language-model cross-entropy, parameter-count or compute scaling, extrapolation from fitted small runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Rows below cover reported scaling results for materials models. Figure 3d compares pretrained potentials but is not a size sweep, so it is not recorded as a scaling result.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps training-set size for materials GNNs (crystal-energy models and NequIP interatomic potentials). The authors say test error falls as a power law with data over roughly 10^3–10^8 examples (Figs 1e, 3a, 3b). This is a new setting for V5, and for V6 through a downstream conductivity-classification task. Parameter count and compute are never swept, and no exponents or fits are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say GNoME test performance improves as a power law with data, consistent with neural scaling laws. They also say scaling data yields emergent out-of-distribution generalization and accurate, transferable zero-shot interatomic potentials. The power-law claims are qualitative, with no exponents given.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales graph neural networks for crystal energies and interatomic potentials, measuring MAE, force error and conductivity-classification error against training-data size. It does not use language-model cross-entropy or sweep parameter count, tokens or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data composition and whether the data contain unique initial structures or intermediate relaxation structures are varied in the reported scaling plots. For robustness, models are trained on 400-K AIMD data and tested at 1,000 K.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal composition sets, training on all relaxation steps ('intermediate structures') versus only the first step ('unique structures') shifts the data-scaling curves. Oversampling first-step structures also improved downstream performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The data-scaling curves of materials potentials depend on what kind of data is counted (unique versus correlated trajectory frames).

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining on GNoME data improves out-of-distribution (1,000 K) force accuracy over from-scratch training at all fine-tuning sizes, even above 1,000 structures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-scale pretraining improves the robustness of fine-tuned potentials to distribution shift.

record.problems: The scaling values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The study scales training data, not parameter count or compute, and tests materials models rather than language models. The transfer comparison does not establish a power-law shape for fine-tuning curves.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3d is a comparison among pretrained potentials on a test set, not a sweep over training size, so it does not bear directly on the listed versions' scaling results.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameters or compute; image, video and repeated-data regimes; whether fine-tuning or transfer curves follow a power law; fitted exponents.
Language-model downstream tasks; predictability from pretraining loss rather than from data size; extrapolation of downstream fits.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no fit-then-predict on larger runs.
Not tested: the architecture is fixed.
Not tested: no exponents or fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Hit rates rise across six active-learning rounds as data grows, from below 6% and 3% to above 80% and 33% (structural and compositional pipelines), and MAE falls from 21 to 11 meV/atom. This is not a controlled sweep but is cited as a benefit of scale.

record.verdict_notes: Only data size is scaled; architecture and parameter count are fixed (the NequIP potential has 16.24M parameters). The power-law statements come from the authors' text and log-log figures without fitted exponents or uncertainty. Single-point comparators (r5, r8, r11) and the transfer comparison (r10) are not scaling evidence. The record's V6 label on r10–r11 is removed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
The effect of depth, width and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

Power-law scaling in image or video models, repeated-data regimes, and whether fine-tuning or transfer curves themselves follow a power law. The study tests data scaling in materials models and reports transfer results, but not those broader cases.
Downstream language-task performance and its relationship to language-model pretraining loss.
Whether scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with setup or fitting choices, and whether curves bend from power laws.
